Historical_Names.Name: Black Star
Historical_Names.Navy: Ordered for the Ghana Navy (never delivered)
Historical_Names.Notes: Intended name for Ghana's flagship and presidential yacht. The order was cancelled after a coup in Ghana in 1966.

Historical_Names.Name: HMS Mermaid (F76)
Historical_Names.Notes: Commissioned 16 May 1973; transferred to Malaysia in 1977.

Historical_Names.Name: KD Hang Tuah (F76)
Historical_Names.Notes: Commissioned 22 July 1977; decommissioned 3 December 2025. Named after Laksamana Hang Tuah. She replaced an earlier KD Hang Tuah, a Loch-class frigate (ex-HMS Loch Insh, F433).

Summary: KD Hang Tuah (F76) served the Royal Malaysian Navy from 1977 to 2025. Built on the Clyde as Black Star for Ghana and commissioned in the Royal Navy as HMS Mermaid, she sailed to Malaysia in 1977 and spent nearly five decades in Malaysian service. Only details confirmed by the sources listed are shown; other fields are marked as still being checked.

Sections.Title: Black Star: built for Ghana
Sections.Body: Ordered by Ghana under President Kwame Nkrumah as Black Star, the ship was to be the Ghana Navy's flagship and a presidential yacht. Yarrow built her at Scotstoun, Glasgow (yard number 2284), basing the design on the Royal Navy's Type 41 and Type 61 frigates but with a flush-decked hull and a single streamlined funnel. After Nkrumah was deposed in a coup the order was cancelled, and Yarrow launched the unfinished ship without ceremony on 29 December 1966. She was then kept at anchor on the Clyde for several years.

Sections.Title: HMS Mermaid, 1973–1977
Sections.Body: Bought for the Royal Navy, she was moved to Portsmouth in April 1972, refitted at Chatham and commissioned as HMS Mermaid (F76) on 16 May 1973. Lightly armed for a frigate, she was sent to the Far East and based at Singapore. Back in home waters she was involved in the Cod Wars, the fisheries dispute between Britain and Iceland. On 20 September 1976 the minesweeper HMS Fittleton sank after colliding with her, with the loss of twelve lives. Her Royal Navy service ended in 1977, when she was transferred to Malaysia.

Sections.Title: The voyage home, 1977
Sections.Body: Commissioned as KD Hang Tuah on 22 July 1977, the ship left Portsmouth on 15 August 1977. According to the panel on board, her ports of call included Jeddah, where the crew spent seven days, performed the Umrah and celebrated Hari Raya Aidilfitri, Muscat and Colombo. She arrived at Port Klang on 14 October and, after two days at Malacca, reached the TLDM base at Woodlands, Singapore, on 18 October 1977.

Sections.Title: Service in the Royal Malaysian Navy
Sections.Body: On 9 September 1984 she carried the navy's royal colours as the TLDM moved from Woodlands to Lumut. In 2018 she was an asset of the 21st Frigate Squadron. Other parts of her Malaysian service record are still being checked against sources.

Sections.Title: Re-engining, 1994–1997
Sections.Body: By the 1990s the ship's eight Admiralty Standard Range diesels, a 1940s design, were worn and genuine spare parts were hard to obtain. After ministerial approval in August 1994, the TLDM awarded Wärtsilä the contract on 22 August 1995 for two 12SW28 main engines and three generator sets. The ship was towed to Malaysia Shipyard & Engineering at Pasir Gudang on 9 October 1995, and the work, costing RM24 million, was accepted by the TLDM in February 1997.

Sections.Title: Decommissioning and the museum project
Sections.Body: Designated the navy's museum ship on 21 November 2018 while remaining in commission, KD Hang Tuah was formally decommissioned at Lumut on 3 December 2025. On 27 July 2026 she was handed to the Perak state government, which plans to open her as the Memorial Muzium Kapal Diraja Hang Tuah in 2027.
